newsitem.title: USA: June housing starts up but may soon level off.
newsitem.headline: June housing starts up but may soon level off.

text.p: Housing starts jumped in June, bolstered by falling interest rates and a strong job market, a government report showed Thursday, though a separate report indicated the job market may be weakening.

Construction of new homes and apartments rose 4.8 percent to an annual rate of 1.45 million last month, the Commerce Department said. That was off the peak rate of 1.55 million reached in February but still a sign of strength in the housing market that points to continued moderate economic growth, analysts said.
The increase followed a revised 6.6 percent drop in May, when starts were running at a 1.39 million rate for the year.

"Building activity is being helped by a stock market wealth effect, relatively low mortgage rates and the general absence of an inventory overhang of unsold new homes," said economist Ken Mayland of KeyCorp Inc. in Cleveland.
Analysts said construction and sales of new homes would probably slow later this summer but stay at healthy levels as consumers remain confident about job prospects and the rising stock market.

"Sales will be robust through the summer into early fall, but then some of the cooling-off that we're beginning to see in the labour market will begin to dampen the housing sector," said Eileen Neely, an economist at Fannie Mae, the government-chartered institution that buys mortgages from lenders and packages them for resale to investors.

A report from the regional Philadelphia Federal Reserve bank Thursday suggested a modestly quickening pace of second-half industrial activity in the Northeast as it rose to 28.1 in July from 25.2 in June, though it was not accompanied by more hiring.

New orders, shipments of finished products and order backlogs all were higher than in June, but a smaller proportion of companies in the Philadelphia region said they were hiring more employees in July than in June.

The Labour Department, in a separate report, said new unemployment claims fell by 28,000 last week to 349,000. But new claims for state jobless benefits had surged the week before as automakers laid off workers to retool plants for 1998 model production.

In addition, the department's four-week moving average of jobless claims, which economists consider a more reliable gauge of the job market, edged up to 348,750 from 348,500. It was the highest since a reading of 349,500 in mid-January, the department said.

"Excluding the effects of the automotive industry, claims still indicate an easing in labour market conditions, as the level has remained above 330,000 for seven consecutive weeks," said Marilyn Schaja at Donaldson, Lufkin and Jenrette Securities Corp. in New York.
Fannie Mae's Neely said housing starts would fall modestly for the full year, to about 1.42 million from 1.47 million last year.
Starts on new single-family homes rose 2.6 percent last month after falling 4.5 percent in May. Construction of apartments rose 12.9 percent, retracing most of May's 13.4 percent decline.
But there were other signs the housing market may lose steam later this year.

The Commerce Department said in its report that new applications for building permits fell 2.6 percent in June, the third straight decline. And the National Association of Home Builders said Wednesday that its index of market activity was unchanged in July from June.

"Overall, the housing market appears stable and healthy," Kent Colton, executive vice president of the builders' group, said Wednesday. But he expects "a gradual slowing of the market and a slight decline in housing starts for the year."

Falling interest rates have helped new homeowners qualify for loans and builders who often borrow to start new projects. The Federal Home Loan Mortgage Corp. said the average rate for a 30-year mortgage fell to 7.69 percent in June from 7.94 percent in May, and rates have fallen further in July.
By region, housing starts jumped 11.2 percent in the South, rose 1.1 percent in the West and edged up 0.7 percent in the Midwest. Starts declined 6.6 percent in the Northeast.
